clinicalPearls: Immune-mediated red cell destruction triggered by a drug or its metabolites
It can mimic warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia clinically and serologically
Implicated drugs classically include some cephalosporins, penicillins and, historically, methyldopa, among others
Mechanisms include drug-dependent antibodies (drug adsorption or immune-complex types) and true drug-independent autoantibodies
The direct antiglobulin test is usually positive, and identifying the culprit drug is central
The mainstay of treatment is stopping the offending drug, with supportive care and transfusion if required
reference.pathophysiology: Drug-induced immune haemolytic anaemia arises when a drug provokes an antibody response that leads to red cell destruction. In the drug-adsorption mechanism the drug binds firmly to the red cell membrane and antibodies target the drug-coated cell; in the immune-complex mechanism drug-antibody complexes attach to red cells and activate complement; and some drugs induce true autoantibodies indistinguishable from those of warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. The result is accelerated clearance of antibody- or complement-coated red cells, causing extravascular or, with strong complement activation, intravascular haemolysis.
additionalInvestigations: Direct antiglobulin test and drug-dependent antibody studies
Detailed drug history including recent additions
Full blood count, reticulocytes and haemolysis markers
Rechallenge avoidance and documentation of the culprit drug
redFlags: Severe or intravascular haemolysis after a new drug
Ongoing exposure to the culprit drug
reference.prognosis: Haemolysis usually resolves after withdrawal of the offending drug, though it can be severe acutely; recovery is generally complete once the drug is stopped and avoided.
pitfalls: Failing to take a thorough drug history and identify the culprit
Mistaking it for idiopathic warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Overlooking oxidative (G6PD-related) drug haemolysis, which is a different mechanism
Re-exposing the patient to the offending drug
management: Immediately stop the implicated drug, the mainstay of treatment, and permanently avoid rechallenge
Provide supportive care with red-cell transfusion for symptomatic or severe anaemia and folate supplementation for ongoing haemolysis
Consider corticosteroids where a drug-independent, true-autoantibody (warm-type) mechanism is identified, as this form behaves like warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Monitor haemoglobin, reticulocytes, the direct antiglobulin test and haemolysis markers to confirm recovery
Support renal function and give intravenous fluids during severe intravascular haemolysis
Clearly document the culprit drug and inform the patient to prevent recurrence
